tname: Concepts of population, sample, sampling methods, outliers
text:
A school has 600 students in four year groups. The number of students in each year group is shown in the table.

| Year group | 10 | 11 | 12 | 13 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Number of students | 120 | 150 | 180 | 150 |

The principal wants to investigate the number of hours of sleep students get on a school night. A stratified sample of 40 students is to be chosen, with year group as the strata.

(a) State whether "number of hours of sleep" is discrete or continuous data. [1]

(b) Calculate the number of Year 12 students that should be in the sample. [2]

(c) Instead of a stratified sample, a teacher suggests asking the first 40 students who arrive at school one morning. Explain why this sample may be biased. [2]
ms:
**(a)** continuous A1

**(b)** $\dfrac{180}{600}\times 40$ (M1)

$= 12$ A1

**(c)** this is a convenience sample, so not every student has an equal chance of being chosen R1

students who arrive earliest may have different sleep habits (e.g. go to bed earlier / live closer / are in a particular year group), so the sample is unlikely to be representative of the whole school R1

Award R1 for identifying the sampling issue and R1 for a valid link to sleep or representativeness.

tname: Concepts of population, sample, sampling methods, outliers
text:
The ages, in years, of 15 members of a running club are listed in order.

$$12,\ 14,\ 15,\ 15,\ 17,\ 18,\ 19,\ 20,\ 21,\ 22,\ 22,\ 24,\ 25,\ 27,\ 41$$

(a) Find

(i) the median age;

(ii) the lower quartile and the upper quartile. [3]

An outlier is defined as a value more than $1.5\times$ IQR below the lower quartile or more than $1.5\times$ IQR above the upper quartile.

(b) Show that the age of 41 is an outlier. [2]

(c) The member aged 41 leaves the club. Find the median age of the remaining 14 members and state, with a reason, whether the mean age increases, decreases or stays the same. [2]
ms:
**(a)(i)** median is the 8th value: $20$ A1

**(ii)** $Q_1 = 15$ A1, $Q_3 = 24$ A1

**(b)** $\text{IQR} = 24 - 15 = 9$ (A1)

$Q_3 + 1.5\times 9 = 24 + 13.5 = 37.5$ M1

$41 > 37.5$ so 41 is an outlier AG

**(c)** median $= \dfrac{19+20}{2} = 19.5$ A1

the mean decreases, because the value removed (41) is greater than the original mean (which is $\frac{312}{15} = 20.8$) R1

tname: Concepts of population, sample, sampling methods, outliers
text:
A factory produces 2400 light bulbs each day. To check quality, a sample of 60 bulbs is taken using systematic sampling. The bulbs are numbered 1 to 2400 in order of production, a starting bulb is chosen at random from the first $k$ bulbs, and then every $k$th bulb is selected.

(a) Identify the population in this investigation. [1]

(b) Find the value of $k$. [1]

(c) The first bulb selected is number 17. Find the number of the fifth bulb selected. [1]

(d) A fault in one of the machines causes every 40th bulb produced to be defective. Explain why systematic sampling could give a misleading estimate of the proportion of defective bulbs. [2]
ms:
**(a)** all 2400 bulbs produced by the factory that day A1

**(b)** $k = \dfrac{2400}{60} = 40$ A1

**(c)** $17 + 4\times 40 = 177$ A1

**(d)** the sampling interval is the same as the period of the fault R1

so the sample would contain either every defective bulb (if the starting number matches the fault) or none of them, giving a proportion of 100% or 0% rather than the true 2.5% R1

tname: Presentation of data: frequency tables, histograms, cumulative frequency, box plots
text:
The histogram shows the time, $t$ minutes, that a group of students spent travelling to school one morning.

![Histogram of travel times with classes of width 10 minutes](qbank/img/gen_math_SL4.2_1.svg)

(a) Write down the modal class. [1]

(b) Find the number of students in the group. [1]

(c) Find an estimate of the mean time. [2]

(d) Find an estimate of the standard deviation of the times. [1]
ms:
Frequencies read from the histogram: $4, 9, 15, 8, 4$.

**(a)** $20 \le t < 30$ A1

**(b)** $4+9+15+8+4 = 40$ A1

**(c)** use of mid-interval values $5, 15, 25, 35, 45$ (M1)

$\dfrac{4(5)+9(15)+15(25)+8(35)+4(45)}{40} = \dfrac{990}{40} = 24.75$ minutes $(24.8)$ A1

**(d)** $\sigma = 11.1$ minutes $(11.0651\ldots)$ A1

Accept $11.2$ (sample standard deviation $11.2066\ldots$). FT from their frequencies.

tname: Presentation of data: frequency tables, histograms, cumulative frequency, box plots
text:
The masses, $m$ grams, of 200 apples picked from an orchard were recorded. The cumulative frequency graph shows the results.

![Cumulative frequency graph of the masses of 200 apples](qbank/img/gen_math_SL4.2_2.svg)

(a) Use the graph to estimate the median mass. [1]

(b) Use the graph to estimate the lower quartile, the upper quartile and hence the interquartile range. [3]

(c) Estimate the number of apples with a mass greater than 190 g. [2]

The masses are summarized in the following table.

| Mass, $m$ (g) | $100\le m<120$ | $120\le m<140$ | $140\le m<160$ | $160\le m<180$ | $180\le m<200$ | $200\le m<220$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frequency | 10 | 30 | $p$ | $q$ | 26 | 8 |

(d) Find the value of $p$ and the value of $q$. [2]

(e) Use the table to find an estimate of the mean mass. [2]

The heaviest 10% of the apples are graded as "premium".

(f) Use the graph to estimate the minimum mass of a premium apple. [2]

(g) Two of the 200 apples are chosen at random, without replacement. Find the probability that both are premium. [2]
ms:
**(a)** median $\approx 157$ g (accept $156$ to $158$) A1

**(b)** $Q_1 \approx 144$ g (accept $143$ to $145$) A1

$Q_3 \approx 173$ g (accept $172$ to $174$) A1

$\text{IQR} \approx 173 - 144 = 29$ g A1

FT from their quartiles.

**(c)** cumulative frequency at 190 g $\approx 182$ (M1)

$200 - 182 = 18$ apples (accept $17$ to $19$) A1

**(d)** $p = 110 - 40 = 70$ A1, $q = 166 - 110 = 56$ A1

(cumulative frequencies read at 140, 160, 180 g are 40, 110, 166)

**(e)** mid-interval values $110, 130, 150, 170, 190, 210$ (M1)

$\bar{m} = \dfrac{31640}{200} = 158.2$ g A1

FT from their $p$ and $q$.

**(f)** top 10% is 20 apples, so read the graph at cumulative frequency $180$ (M1)

minimum mass $\approx 189$ g (accept $188$ to $190$) A1

**(g)** $\dfrac{20}{200}\times\dfrac{19}{199}$ (M1)

$= \dfrac{19}{1990} = 0.00955$ $(0.00954773\ldots)$ A1

tname: Presentation of data: frequency tables, histograms, cumulative frequency, box plots
text:
Two groups of students, A and B, each completed the same puzzle. The box-and-whisker diagrams show the times taken, in seconds.

![Box-and-whisker diagrams for groups A and B](qbank/img/gen_math_SL4.2_3.svg)

(a) Write down the median time for group A. [1]

(b) Find the interquartile range of the times for group B. [2]

(c) Write down the percentage of students in group A who took longer than 27 seconds. [1]

(d) By comparing the interquartile ranges, state which group had the more consistent times. [1]
ms:
**(a)** $22$ seconds A1

**(b)** $Q_3 - Q_1 = 28 - 20$ (M1)

$= 8$ seconds A1

**(c)** $25\%$ A1

**(d)** group B, since its IQR ($8$) is smaller than that of group A ($27-18=9$) A1

Note: the range of group B ($25$) is larger than that of group A ($23$), so an answer based on the ranges scores A0. FT from (b).

tname: Presentation of data: frequency tables, histograms, cumulative frequency, box plots
text:
The table shows the number of goals, $x$, scored by a hockey team in each of its matches in one season.

| Goals, $x$ | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Number of matches | 5 | 7 | $k$ | 6 | 4 |

The mean number of goals per match is $2.9$.

(a) Find the value of $k$. [3]

(b) Find the median number of goals per match. [2]

(c) Write down the modal number of goals per match. [1]
ms:
**(a)** $\dfrac{5 + 14 + 3k + 24 + 20}{22 + k} = 2.9$ M1A1

$63 + 3k = 63.8 + 2.9k \Rightarrow 0.1k = 0.8$

$k = 8$ A1

**(b)** $30$ matches, so the median is the mean of the 15th and 16th values (M1)

cumulative frequencies $5, 12, 20, \ldots$ so both are $3$: median $= 3$ A1

**(c)** $3$ A1

FT from their $k$ in (b) and (c).

tname: Presentation of data: frequency tables, histograms, cumulative frequency, box plots
text:
The lengths, in cm, of 80 fish caught in a lake were measured. The box-and-whisker diagram summarizes the results. The cross shows a single fish of length 52 cm.

![Box-and-whisker diagram of fish lengths with one outlier at 52 cm](qbank/img/gen_math_SL4.2_5.svg)

(a) Write down the median length. [1]

(b) Write down the interquartile range. [1]

(c) Show that the fish of length 52 cm is an outlier. [2]

(d) Estimate the number of fish with lengths between 24 cm and 32 cm. [1]

(e) The person who recorded the data says the 52 cm fish should be removed because it is an outlier. Comment on this suggestion. [1]
ms:
**(a)** $28$ cm A1

**(b)** $32 - 24 = 8$ cm A1

**(c)** $Q_3 + 1.5\times\text{IQR} = 32 + 1.5(8)$ M1

$= 44$, and $52 > 44$ so 52 is an outlier A1

Award M1A0 if the boundary is not compared with 52.

**(d)** half of the fish lie between $Q_1$ and $Q_3$: $40$ A1

**(e)** an outlier should only be removed if it is an error (e.g. a recording mistake or a fish from a different species); a genuine large fish is valid data and should be kept R1

tname: Measures of central tendency and dispersion
text:
The daily maximum temperatures, $C$ degrees Celsius, in a city during June have a mean of $20$ and a standard deviation of $4$.

The temperatures are converted to degrees Fahrenheit, $F$, using $F = 1.8C + 32$.

(a) Find the mean of the temperatures in degrees Fahrenheit. [2]

(b) Find the standard deviation of the temperatures in degrees Fahrenheit. [2]

(c) Hence find the variance of the temperatures in degrees Fahrenheit. [1]
ms:
**(a)** $1.8(20) + 32$ (M1)

$= 68$ A1

**(b)** adding 32 does not change the spread; multiplying by 1.8 multiplies it by 1.8 (M1)

$1.8\times 4 = 7.2$ A1

**(c)** $7.2^2 = 51.84$ A1

FT from (b).

tname: Measures of central tendency and dispersion
text:
Class A has 18 students and class B has 12 students. They all sat the same test.

The mean score for class A was 64. The mean score for the 30 students together was 67.6.

(a) Find the mean score for class B. [3]

(b) One more student sits the test and is added to the combined group. The mean score for the 31 students is now 68. Find the score of this student. [2]

tname: Measures of central tendency and dispersion
text:
The times, in minutes, that ten customers waited to be served in a bank were

$$23,\ 31,\ 27,\ 35,\ 29,\ 41,\ 26,\ 33,\ 30,\ 38.$$

(a) Find the mean waiting time. [1]

(b) Find the standard deviation of the waiting times. [1]

(c) Find the median waiting time. [1]

(d) Find the interquartile range of the waiting times. [2]
ms:
**(a)** $31.3$ minutes A1

**(b)** $5.27$ minutes $(5.27351\ldots)$ A1

Accept $5.56$ (sample standard deviation).

**(c)** $30.5$ minutes A1

**(d)** $Q_1 = 27,\ Q_3 = 35$ (A1)

$\text{IQR} = 8$ minutes A1

tname: Measures of central tendency and dispersion
text:
Five positive integers $a, b, c, d, e$, where $a \le b \le c \le d \le e$, have

- a unique mode of $8$,
- a median of $7$,
- a mean of $6$,
- a range of $7$.

(a) Find the five integers. [4]

(b) A sixth positive integer, $x$, is added to the list. The mean of the six integers is still $6$. Find $x$ and the median of the six integers. [2]
ms:
**(a)** median $c = 7$ A1

mode is 8, which is greater than the median, so $d = e = 8$ R1

sum $= 30$, so $a + b = 30 - 7 - 16 = 7$, and range: $8 - a = 7 \Rightarrow a = 1$ M1

so $b = 6$; the integers are $1, 6, 7, 8, 8$ A1

**(b)** $x = 6$ A1

ordered list $1, 6, 6, 7, 8, 8$: median $= 6.5$ A1

tname: Measures of central tendency and dispersion
text:
For a set of 10 observations, $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{10} x_i = 360$ and $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{10} x_i^2 = 13200$.

(a) Find the mean of the observations. [1]

(b) Show that the variance of the observations is 24 and hence find the standard deviation. [2]

An eleventh observation, $x_{11} = 36$, is added to the data.

(c) Write down the mean of the 11 observations. [1]

(d) Find the standard deviation of the 11 observations. [2]
ms:
**(a)** $\bar{x} = \dfrac{360}{10} = 36$ A1

**(b)** $\sigma^2 = \dfrac{13200}{10} - 36^2 = 1320 - 1296 = 24$ M1AG

$\sigma = \sqrt{24} = 4.90$ $(4.89897\ldots)$ A1

**(c)** $36$ A1

**(d)** new $\sum x^2 = 13200 + 36^2 = 14496$ (M1)

$\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{14496}{11} - 36^2} = \sqrt{21.818\ldots} = 4.67$ $(4.67099\ldots)$ A1

Alternative: the new value equals the mean, so $\sum(x-\bar{x})^2 = 240$ is unchanged and $\sigma = \sqrt{240/11}$.

tname: Correlation and the regression line of y on x
text:
Eight students recorded the number of hours, $x$, they spent revising for a test and their test score, $y$.

| $x$ (hours) | 2 | 4 | 5 | 7 | 8 | 10 | 12 | 13 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $y$ (score) | 38 | 47 | 46 | 55 | 58 | 66 | 68 | 77 |

The data are shown on the scatter diagram.

![Scatter diagram of test score against hours of revision](qbank/img/gen_math_SL4.4_1.svg)

(a) Describe the correlation between $x$ and $y$. [1]

(b) Find the value of Pearson's product-moment correlation coefficient, $r$. [2]

(c) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$, in the form $y = ax + b$. [2]

(d) Find $\bar{x}$ and $\bar{y}$, and verify that the point $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$ lies on the regression line. [2]

(e) Use your regression line to estimate the score of a student who revised for 9 hours. [2]

(f) Explain why the regression line should not be used to estimate the score of a student who revised for 20 hours. [1]

(g) Interpret, in context, the value of $a$. [1]

(h) A ninth student revised for 6 hours and scored 90. Without further calculation, state the effect of including this student on the value of $r$. [1]
ms:
**(a)** strong positive (linear) correlation A1

**(b)** $r = 0.988$ $(0.988275\ldots)$ A2

**(c)** $y = 3.31x + 31.6$ $(a = 3.31168\ldots,\ b = 31.6233\ldots)$ A1A1

**(d)** $\bar{x} = 7.625,\ \bar{y} = 56.875$ A1

$3.31168\ldots(7.625) + 31.6233\ldots = 56.875$, so the point lies on the line R1

**(e)** $y = 3.31168\ldots(9) + 31.6233\ldots$ (M1)

$= 61.4$ $(61.4285\ldots)$ A1

Accept $61.4$ to $61.5$ from 3 s.f. coefficients. FT from (c).

**(f)** 20 hours is outside the range of the data ($2 \le x \le 13$), so this would be extrapolation and unreliable R1

**(g)** for each extra hour of revision, the score increases by about 3.3 marks (on average) A1

**(h)** $r$ would decrease (the correlation becomes weaker) A1

tname: Correlation and the regression line of y on x
text:
A researcher measures two variables, $x$ and $y$, for 10 people. The regression line of $y$ on $x$ is $y = 2.4x + 13$ and Pearson's correlation coefficient is $r = 0.87$.

The mean of the $x$ values is $15$.

(a) Find the mean of the $y$ values. [2]

(b) Hence find $\displaystyle\sum y$. [1]

(c) Use the regression line to estimate $y$ when $x = 20$, given that $x = 20$ lies within the range of the data. [1]

(d) Explain why this regression line should not be used to estimate $x$ when $y = 70$. [1]
ms:
**(a)** the regression line passes through $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$ (M1)

$\bar{y} = 2.4(15) + 13 = 49$ A1

**(b)** $\sum y = 10\times 49 = 490$ A1

**(c)** $2.4(20) + 13 = 61$ A1

**(d)** the line of $y$ on $x$ is for estimating $y$ from $x$; to estimate $x$ from $y$ the regression line of $x$ on $y$ is needed R1

tname: Correlation and the regression line of y on x
text:
The four scatter diagrams A, B, C and D each show 20 pairs of data.

![Four scatter diagrams labelled A to D](qbank/img/gen_math_SL4.4_3.svg)

The values of Pearson's correlation coefficient for the four diagrams, in no particular order, are

$$0.96,\quad -0.97,\quad 0.05,\quad -0.71.$$

(a) Match each diagram to its value of $r$. [3]

(b) State which diagram shows the strongest linear correlation. [1]
ms:
**(a)** A: $-0.71$, B: $0.96$, C: $-0.97$, D: $0.05$

Award A3 for all four correct, A2 for two correct, A1 for one correct (exactly three correct is not possible).

**(b)** C A1

FT from (a) only if their value for C has the largest $|r|$.

tname: Correlation and the regression line of y on x
text:
A shop records the midday temperature, $T$ °C, and the number of ice creams sold, $S$, on eight days.

| $T$ (°C) | 14 | 16 | 18 | 20 | 22 | 24 | 26 | 28 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $S$ | 118 | 138 | 147 | 165 | 40 | 186 | 209 | 218 |

(a) Find Pearson's product-moment correlation coefficient for all eight days. [2]

(b) Identify the day that does not fit the pattern, and suggest a reason for it. [1]

The manager removes this day from the data.

(c) For the remaining seven days, find

(i) the new value of the correlation coefficient;

(ii) the equation of the regression line of $S$ on $T$. [3]

(d) Use your answer to (c)(ii) to estimate the number of ice creams sold on a day when the midday temperature is 25 °C. [1]
ms:
**(a)** $r = 0.534$ $(0.534403\ldots)$ A2

**(b)** $(22, 40)$: e.g. a recording error (140 written as 40), or the shop was closed for part of the day R1

**(c)(i)** $r = 0.996$ $(0.995976\ldots)$ A1

**(ii)** $S = 7.05T + 21.7$ $(7.04623\ldots T + 21.75)$ A1A1

**(d)** $7.04623\ldots(25) + 21.75 = 197.9\ldots$, so about $198$ ice creams A1

Accept $198$ or $197.9$. FT from (c)(ii).

tname: Correlation and the regression line of y on x
text:
The table shows the age, $x$ years, and the selling price, $y$ thousand euros, of six used cars of the same model.

| $x$ (years) | 1 | 2 | 3 | 5 | 6 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $y$ (thousand euros) | 18.5 | 15.4 | 15.2 | 11.0 | 10.8 | 6.9 |

(a) Find the value of Pearson's product-moment correlation coefficient, $r$. [2]

(b) Describe the relationship between age and selling price. [1]

(c) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [2]

(d) Interpret the gradient of the regression line in context. [1]

(e) Use the regression line to estimate the selling price of a car of this model that is 15 years old, and comment on your answer. [2]
ms:
**(a)** $r = -0.986$ $(-0.986375\ldots)$ A2

**(b)** strong negative (linear) correlation: older cars sell for less A1

**(c)** $y = -1.56x + 19.5$ $(-1.55789\ldots x + 19.4578\ldots)$ A1A1

**(d)** the price falls by about 1560 euros (1.56 thousand euros) for each additional year of age A1

**(e)** $-1.55789\ldots(15) + 19.4578\ldots = -3.91$ (thousand euros) A1

a negative price is impossible; 15 years is outside the data range so this extrapolation is not valid R1

tname: Concepts of probability, sample space, expected outcomes
text:
Two fair six-sided dice, each numbered 1 to 6, are thrown.

(a) Find the probability that the sum of the two scores is 8. [2]

(b) Find the probability that the product of the two scores is even. [2]

(c) The two dice are thrown 180 times. Find the expected number of times the sum is 8. [1]
ms:
**(a)** 36 equally likely outcomes; sum 8: $(2,6),(3,5),(4,4),(5,3),(6,2)$ (M1)

$\dfrac{5}{36}$ A1

**(b)** product odd only if both odd: $\dfrac{3}{6}\times\dfrac{3}{6} = \dfrac14$ (M1)

$P(\text{even}) = 1 - \dfrac14 = \dfrac34$ A1

**(c)** $180\times\dfrac{5}{36} = 25$ A1

FT from (a).

tname: Concepts of probability, sample space, expected outcomes
text:
A fair spinner is divided into four sectors. The angle of each sector is shown on the diagram.

![Spinner with Red 120 degrees, Blue 90 degrees, Green 60 degrees, Yellow 90 degrees](qbank/img/gen_math_SL4.5_2.svg)

(a) Find the probability that the spinner lands on green. [1]

(b) Find the probability that the spinner does not land on blue. [1]

(c) The spinner is spun 240 times. Find the expected number of times it lands on red. [1]

(d) The spinner is spun twice. Find the probability that it lands on the same colour both times. [3]
ms:
**(a)** $\dfrac{60}{360} = \dfrac16$ A1

**(b)** $1 - \dfrac{90}{360} = \dfrac34$ A1

**(c)** $240\times\dfrac13 = 80$ A1

**(d)** $P(R)=\frac13,\ P(B)=\frac14,\ P(G)=\frac16,\ P(Y)=\frac14$

$\left(\dfrac13\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac14\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac16\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac14\right)^2$ M1A1

$= \dfrac{16 + 9 + 4 + 9}{144} = \dfrac{38}{144} = \dfrac{19}{72}$ A1

Award M1 for squaring and adding probabilities, A1 for all four correct terms.

tname: Concepts of probability, sample space, expected outcomes
text:
A six-sided die is thought to be biased. It is thrown 200 times and the results are recorded.

| Score | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frequency | 28 | 30 | 32 | 34 | 26 | 50 |

(a) Use the results to estimate the probability of throwing a 6. [1]

(b) Use the results to estimate the probability of throwing an odd number. [2]

(c) The die is thrown 1500 more times. Use your answer to (a) to find the expected number of sixes. [1]

(d) Suggest how the estimate in (a) could be made more reliable. [1]
ms:
**(a)** $\dfrac{50}{200} = 0.25$ A1

**(b)** $\dfrac{28 + 32 + 26}{200}$ (M1)

$= \dfrac{86}{200} = 0.43$ A1

**(c)** $1500\times 0.25 = 375$ A1

**(d)** throw the die many more times (a larger number of trials) R1

tname: Concepts of probability, sample space, expected outcomes
text:
A fair four-sided die, numbered 1 to 4, and a fair six-sided die, numbered 1 to 6, are thrown together. The score is the sum of the two numbers shown.

(a) Find the probability that the score is 7. [2]

(b) Find the probability that the score is at least 7. [2]

(c) Find the probability that at least one of the dice shows a 4. [2]

(d) Given that the score is a prime number, find the probability that the four-sided die shows a 1. [2]
ms:
24 equally likely outcomes.

**(a)** $(1,6),(2,5),(3,4),(4,3)$ (M1)

$\dfrac{4}{24} = \dfrac16$ A1

**(b)** score 7: 4, score 8: 3, score 9: 2, score 10: 1 (M1)

$\dfrac{10}{24} = \dfrac{5}{12}$ A1

**(c)** $1 - \dfrac34\times\dfrac56$ (M1)

$= 1 - \dfrac{15}{24} = \dfrac{9}{24} = \dfrac38$ A1

**(d)** prime scores 2, 3, 5, 7: number of outcomes $1 + 2 + 4 + 4 = 11$ (A1)

with the four-sided die showing 1: $(1,1),(1,2),(1,4),(1,6)$, so $\dfrac{4}{11}$ A1

tname: Venn diagrams, tree diagrams, combined, mutually exclusive, conditional and independent events
text:
In a group of 50 students, $M$ is the event that a student studies music and $A$ is the event that a student studies art. The Venn diagram shows the number of students in each region.

![Venn diagram with 12 in M only, 8 in both, 10 in A only and 20 outside](qbank/img/gen_math_SL4.6_1.svg)

A student is chosen at random from the group.

(a) Find the probability that the student studies art. [1]

(b) Find $\mathrm{P}\big((M\cup A)'\big)$. [1]

(c) Find $\mathrm{P}(M \mid A')$. [2]

(d) Two different students are chosen at random. Find the probability that both study music and art. [2]

tname: Venn diagrams, tree diagrams, combined, mutually exclusive, conditional and independent events
text:
A group of 70 students were asked whether they play football ($F$), basketball ($B$) or tennis ($T$). The Venn diagram shows the results.

![Three-set Venn diagram with regions 2x, x+3, 9, 5, 4, x, 3 and 6 outside](qbank/img/gen_math_SL4.6_2.svg)

(a) Find the value of $x$. [2]

A student is chosen at random.

(b) Find the probability that the student plays exactly two of the three sports. [2]

(c) Given that the student plays basketball, find the probability that the student also plays tennis. [2]

tname: Venn diagrams, tree diagrams, combined, mutually exclusive, conditional and independent events
text:
A bag contains 6 red balls and 4 green balls. Two balls are taken at random from the bag, one after the other, without replacement. The tree diagram shows the possible outcomes.

![Tree diagram for two draws without replacement with missing probabilities p and q](qbank/img/gen_math_SL4.6_3.svg)

(a) Write down the value of $p$ and the value of $q$. [2]

(b) Find the probability that the two balls are different colours. [2]

(c) Given that the two balls are different colours, find the probability that the first ball was red. [2]
ms:
**(a)** $p = \dfrac49$ A1, $q = \dfrac69 \left(=\dfrac23\right)$ A1

**(b)** $\dfrac{6}{10}\times\dfrac49 + \dfrac{4}{10}\times\dfrac69$ M1

$= \dfrac{48}{90} = \dfrac{8}{15}$ A1

**(c)** $\dfrac{24/90}{48/90}$ M1

$= \dfrac12$ A1

FT from (b).

tname: Venn diagrams, tree diagrams, combined, mutually exclusive, conditional and independent events
text:
A medical condition, $D$, affects 2% of a population. A test for the condition gives either a positive ($P$) or negative ($N$) result.

- If a person has the condition, the probability that the test is positive is 0.95.
- If a person does not have the condition, the probability that the test is positive is 0.10.

The information is shown on the tree diagram.

![Tree diagram for the condition and the test result with missing values a and b](qbank/img/gen_math_SL4.6_4.svg)

(a) Write down the value of $a$ and the value of $b$. [2]

(b) A person is chosen at random and tested. Find the probability that the test is positive. [2]

(c) Given that the test is positive, find the probability that the person has the condition. [3]

tname: Venn diagrams, tree diagrams, combined, mutually exclusive, conditional and independent events
text:
Events $A$ and $B$ are such that $\mathrm{P}(A) = 0.4$ and $\mathrm{P}(B) = 0.3$.

(a) Find $\mathrm{P}(A\cup B)$ if $A$ and $B$ are independent. [2]

(b) Find $\mathrm{P}(A\cup B)$ if $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive. [1]

(c) Find $\mathrm{P}(A\cap B)$ if $\mathrm{P}(A\cup B) = 0.6$. [1]

tname: Venn diagrams, tree diagrams, combined, mutually exclusive, conditional and independent events
text:
Ann and Bob play a game. They take turns to throw a fair six-sided die, with Ann throwing first. The first player to throw a 6 wins the game.

The tree diagram shows the start of the game.

![Tree diagram for the first throws of Ann and Bob](qbank/img/gen_math_SL4.6_6.svg)

(a) Write down the probability that Ann wins on her first throw. [1]

(b) Find the probability that Bob wins on his first throw. [2]

(c) Show that the probability that Ann wins on her second throw is $\dfrac{25}{216}$. [2]

(d) Find the probability that Ann wins the game. [4]

(e) Given that Ann wins the game, find the probability that she won on her first throw. [3]

(f) Ann and Bob play three games. The games are independent. Find the probability that Bob wins at least one of the three games. [2]
ms:
**(a)** $\dfrac16$ A1

**(b)** $\dfrac56\times\dfrac16$ M1

$= \dfrac{5}{36}$ A1

**(c)** both miss once, then Ann throws a 6: $\dfrac56\times\dfrac56\times\dfrac16$ M1A1

$= \dfrac{25}{216}$ AG

**(d)** $\mathrm{P}(\text{Ann wins}) = \dfrac16 + \dfrac16\left(\dfrac{25}{36}\right) + \dfrac16\left(\dfrac{25}{36}\right)^2 + \cdots$ M1

geometric series with $u_1 = \dfrac16$, $r = \dfrac{25}{36}$ (A1)

$S_\infty = \dfrac{\frac16}{1 - \frac{25}{36}}$ M1

$= \dfrac{\frac16}{\frac{11}{36}} = \dfrac{6}{11}$ A1

**(e)** $\mathrm{P}(\text{first throw}\mid\text{Ann wins}) = \dfrac{\frac16}{\frac{6}{11}}$ M1A1

$= \dfrac{11}{36}$ A1

FT from (d).

**(f)** $\mathrm{P}(\text{Bob wins a game}) = \dfrac{5}{11}$, so $\mathrm{P}(\text{Bob wins none}) = \left(\dfrac{6}{11}\right)^3$ (M1)

$1 - \dfrac{216}{1331} = \dfrac{1115}{1331}$ A1

FT from (d).

tname: Venn diagrams, tree diagrams, combined, mutually exclusive, conditional and independent events
text:
The table shows how 150 students in Years 11 and 12 travel to school.

| | Walk | Bus | Car | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Year 11 | 25 | 30 | 15 | 70 |
| Year 12 | 20 | 25 | 35 | 80 |
| Total | 45 | 55 | 50 | 150 |

A student is chosen at random.

(a) Find the probability that the student travels by car. [1]

(b) Given that the student travels by bus, find the probability that the student is in Year 12. [2]

(c) Find the probability that the student walks or is in Year 11 (or both). [2]

(d) Determine whether the events "the student walks" and "the student is in Year 11" are independent. [2]
ms:
**(a)** $\dfrac{50}{150} = \dfrac13$ A1

**(b)** $\dfrac{25}{55}$ (M1)

$= \dfrac{5}{11}$ A1

**(c)** $\dfrac{45 + 70 - 25}{150}$ (M1)

$= \dfrac{90}{150} = \dfrac35$ A1

**(d)** $\mathrm{P}(W)\times\mathrm{P}(Y11) = \dfrac{45}{150}\times\dfrac{70}{150} = \dfrac{7}{50}$ and $\mathrm{P}(W\cap Y11) = \dfrac{25}{150} = \dfrac16$ M1

$\dfrac16 \ne \dfrac{7}{50}$, so the events are not independent A1

Accept a comparison of $\mathrm{P}(W\mid Y11) = \frac{25}{70}$ with $\mathrm{P}(W) = \frac{45}{150}$.

tname: Discrete random variables and their probability distributions, expected value
text:
The probability distribution of a discrete random variable $X$ is shown in the table.

| $x$ | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{P}(X = x)$ | 0.1 | $2k$ | 0.3 | $k$ |

(a) Find the value of $k$. [2]

(b) Find $\mathrm{E}(X)$. [2]

tname: Discrete random variables and their probability distributions, expected value
text:
The probability distribution of a discrete random variable $X$ is given by

$$\mathrm{P}(X = x) = k(x + 1), \quad x = 0, 1, 2, 3.$$

(a) Show that $k = 0.1$. [2]

(b) Find $\mathrm{P}(X \ge 2)$. [1]

(c) Find $\mathrm{E}(X)$. [2]

tname: Discrete random variables and their probability distributions, expected value
text:
In a game, a player pays €3 to throw a fair six-sided die once.

- If the score is 6, the player receives €$k$.
- If the score is 4 or 5, the player receives €2.
- Otherwise, the player receives nothing.

(a) Find, in terms of $k$, the expected amount the player receives in one game. [2]

(b) Find the value of $k$ for which the game is fair. [2]

(c) The organizer sets $k = 8$. Find the expected total loss of a player who plays 30 games. [2]
ms:
**(a)** $\dfrac16 k + \dfrac26(2) + \dfrac36(0)$ M1

$= \dfrac{k + 4}{6}$ A1

**(b)** fair game: $\dfrac{k + 4}{6} = 3$ M1

$k = 14$ A1

**(c)** expected gain per game $= \dfrac{12}{6} - 3 = -1$ euro (M1)

expected total loss $= 30$ euros A1

FT from (a).

tname: Discrete random variables and their probability distributions, expected value
text:
A bag contains 4 red and 6 blue counters. Two counters are taken at random from the bag without replacement. Let $X$ be the number of red counters taken.

(a) Find $\mathrm{P}(X = 0)$ and $\mathrm{P}(X = 2)$. [3]

(b) Find $\mathrm{P}(X = 1)$. [1]

(c) Find $\mathrm{E}(X)$. [2]
ms:
**(a)** $\mathrm{P}(X=0) = \dfrac{6}{10}\times\dfrac59$ (M1)

$= \dfrac{30}{90} = \dfrac13$ A1

$\mathrm{P}(X=2) = \dfrac{4}{10}\times\dfrac39 = \dfrac{12}{90} = \dfrac{2}{15}$ A1

**(b)** $1 - \dfrac13 - \dfrac{2}{15} = \dfrac{8}{15}$ A1

Accept $2\times\frac{4}{10}\times\frac69 = \frac{48}{90}$.

**(c)** $0\left(\dfrac13\right) + 1\left(\dfrac{8}{15}\right) + 2\left(\dfrac{2}{15}\right)$ (M1)

$= \dfrac{12}{15} = \dfrac45$ A1

tname: Discrete random variables and their probability distributions, expected value
text:
The discrete random variable $X$ has the probability distribution shown.

| $x$ | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{P}(X = x)$ | 0.2 | $a$ | $b$ | 0.1 |

It is known that $\mathrm{E}(X) = 1.5$.

(a) Find the value of $a$ and the value of $b$. [4]

Two independent observations, $X_1$ and $X_2$, are taken.

(b) Find the probability that $X_1 + X_2 = 3$. [2]

(c) Given that $X_1 + X_2 = 3$, find the probability that one of the observations is 0. [2]

tname: Binomial distribution
text:
The random variable $X$ follows a binomial distribution, $X \sim \mathrm{B}(12, 0.3)$.

(a) Find $\mathrm{P}(X = 4)$. [2]

(b) Find $\mathrm{P}(X \le 3)$. [2]

(c) Write down $\mathrm{E}(X)$. [1]

tname: Binomial distribution
text:
A multiple-choice test has 20 questions. Each question has four possible answers, only one of which is correct. Sam guesses the answer to every question at random.

(a) Write down the expected number of questions Sam answers correctly. [1]

(b) Find the probability that Sam answers exactly 5 questions correctly. [2]

(c) The pass mark is 8. Find the probability that Sam passes the test. [2]
ms:
Let $X$ be the number of correct answers, $X \sim \mathrm{B}(20, 0.25)$. (M1) may be implied.

**(a)** $20\times 0.25 = 5$ A1

**(b)** $\mathrm{P}(X = 5)$ (M1)

$= 0.202$ $(0.202331\ldots)$ A1

**(c)** $\mathrm{P}(X \ge 8) = 1 - \mathrm{P}(X \le 7)$ (M1)

$= 0.102$ $(0.101811\ldots)$ A1

Award (M1)A0 for $1 - \mathrm{P}(X\le 8) = 0.0409$.

tname: Binomial distribution
text:
The probability that a component made by a machine is defective is 0.08. Components are made independently of each other.

(a) A sample of 20 components is chosen. Find the probability that at least one is defective. [2]

(b) Find the least number of components, $n$, that must be chosen so that the probability of at least one being defective is greater than 0.95. [3]

tname: Binomial distribution
text:
The probability that a seed of a particular type germinates is 0.85, independently of all other seeds. The seeds are sold in packets of 20. Let $X$ be the number of seeds in a packet that germinate.

(a) Find the mean and the variance of $X$. [2]

(b) Find the probability that exactly 17 seeds in a packet germinate. [2]

(c) Find the probability that at least 18 seeds in a packet germinate. [2]

(d) Given that at least 18 seeds in a packet germinate, find the probability that all 20 germinate. [3]

A garden centre buys 10 packets. A packet is described as "high quality" if at least 18 of its seeds germinate.

(e) Find the probability that exactly 3 of the 10 packets are high quality. [3]

(f) Find the probability that at least 2 of the 10 packets are high quality. [2]

tname: Binomial distribution
text:
The random variable $X \sim \mathrm{B}(n, p)$ has mean $6$ and variance $4.2$.

(a) Find the value of $p$ and the value of $n$. [4]

(b) Find $\mathrm{P}(X = 6)$. [1]

(c) Find $\mathrm{P}(X > 6)$. [1]

tname: The normal distribution
text:
The random variable $X$ is normally distributed with mean 50 and standard deviation 4.

(a) Find $\mathrm{P}(X < 44)$. [2]

(b) The diagram shows the graph of the probability density function of $X$. Find the area of the shaded region. [2]

![Normal curve with the region between 46 and 56 shaded](qbank/img/gen_math_SL4.9_1.svg)

tname: The normal distribution
text:
The random variable $X$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu$. It is known that $\mathrm{P}(X < 20) = 0.15$ and $\mathrm{P}(X > 40) = 0.15$, as shown in the diagram.

![Normal curve with both tails beyond 20 and 40 shaded, each of area 0.15](qbank/img/gen_math_SL4.9_2.svg)

(a) Write down the value of $\mu$. [1]

(b) Find $\mathrm{P}(20 < X < 40)$. [2]

(c) Find $\mathrm{P}(30 < X < 40)$. [1]

(d) It is also known that $\mathrm{P}(X < 25) = 0.3$. Find $\mathrm{P}(25 < X < 35)$. [2]

tname: The normal distribution
text:
The masses of bags of flour filled by a machine are normally distributed with mean 500 g and standard deviation 8 g.

(a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen bag has a mass of less than 490 g. [2]

(b) A sample of 50 bags is taken. Find the expected number of bags in the sample with mass less than 490 g. [2]

(c) Two bags are chosen at random. Find the probability that both bags have a mass greater than 510 g. [2]

tname: The normal distribution
text:
The scores in an aptitude test are normally distributed with mean 120 and standard deviation 15.

(a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen candidate scores more than 140. [2]

(b) The top 10% of candidates receive an award. Find the minimum score needed to receive an award. [2]

(c) Find the two scores, symmetric about the mean, between which the middle 50% of scores lie. [2]

tname: The normal distribution
text:
The lengths, $L$ mm, of bolts made in a factory are normally distributed with mean 45.0 mm and standard deviation 0.4 mm. A bolt is acceptable if its length is between 44.2 mm and 45.6 mm.

(a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen bolt is acceptable. [2]

(b) Find the length that is exceeded by 10% of the bolts. [2]

(c) Bolts are packed in boxes of 12. Find the probability that a box contains at least 10 acceptable bolts. [3]

(d) Given that a bolt is acceptable, find the probability that its length is greater than 45.0 mm. [3]

(e) Find the interquartile range of the lengths of the bolts. [3]

tname: Regression line of x on y
text:
A coach recorded the number of hours of training per week, $x$, and the best 100 m time, $y$ seconds, for seven sprinters.

| $x$ (hours) | 3 | 5 | 6 | 8 | 9 | 11 | 12 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $y$ (seconds) | 15.8 | 14.7 | 14.9 | 13.8 | 13.6 | 12.6 | 12.7 |

(a) Find the value of Pearson's product-moment correlation coefficient. [2]

(b) Find the equation of the regression line of $x$ on $y$, in the form $x = cy + d$. [2]

(c) A sprinter wants to achieve a time of 13.0 seconds. Use your answer to (b) to estimate the number of hours of training per week this sprinter needs. [1]

(d) Explain why the regression line of $y$ on $x$ should not be used to answer part (c). [1]
ms:
**(a)** $r = -0.983$ $(-0.982861\ldots)$ A2

**(b)** $x = -2.70y + 45.6$ $(c = -2.70265\ldots,\ d = 45.5900\ldots)$ A1A1

**(c)** $-2.70265\ldots(13.0) + 45.5900\ldots = 10.5$ hours $(10.4555\ldots)$ A1

Accept $10.5$ or $10.4$ from 3 s.f. coefficients. FT from (b).

**(d)** the $y$ on $x$ line minimizes errors in $y$; to estimate $x$ from a given $y$ the line of $x$ on $y$ must be used (the two lines are different unless $|r| = 1$) R1

tname: Regression line of x on y
text:
For a set of bivariate data, the regression line of $y$ on $x$ has equation $y = 0.8x + 10$ and the regression line of $x$ on $y$ has equation $x = 0.9y - 2$.

(a) Find the mean of the $x$ values and the mean of the $y$ values. [3]

(b) Use the appropriate line to estimate the value of $y$ when $x = 30$. [2]

(c) Use the appropriate line to estimate the value of $x$ when $y = 40$. [1]
ms:
**(a)** both lines pass through $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$ (M1)

$x = 0.9(0.8x + 10) - 2 \Rightarrow 0.28x = 7$ M1

$\bar{x} = 25,\ \bar{y} = 30$ A1

**(b)** use of $y$ on $x$ line: $0.8(30) + 10$ (M1)

$= 34$ A1

Award (M1)A0 for use of the $x$ on $y$ line.

**(c)** $x = 0.9(40) - 2 = 34$ A1

tname: Formal conditional probability and independence tests
text:
Events $A$ and $B$ are such that $\mathrm{P}(A) = 0.5$, $\mathrm{P}(B) = 0.4$ and $\mathrm{P}(A\mid B) = 0.3$.

(a) Find $\mathrm{P}(A\cap B)$. [2]

(b) Find $\mathrm{P}(A\cup B)$. [2]

(c) Determine whether $A$ and $B$ are independent. Justify your answer. [2]
ms:
**(a)** $\mathrm{P}(A\cap B) = \mathrm{P}(A\mid B)\,\mathrm{P}(B) = 0.3\times 0.4$ (M1)

$= 0.12$ A1

**(b)** $0.5 + 0.4 - 0.12$ (M1)

$= 0.78$ A1

**(c)** $\mathrm{P}(A\mid B) = 0.3 \ne 0.5 = \mathrm{P}(A)$ R1

so $A$ and $B$ are not independent A1

Accept $\mathrm{P}(A)\mathrm{P}(B) = 0.2 \ne 0.12$. Do not award A1 without R1.

tname: Formal conditional probability and independence tests
text:
In a survey of 100 students, $S$ is the event that a student is a member of a sports club and $G$ is the event that a student wears glasses. The results are shown in the table.

| | $G$ | $G'$ |
|---|---|---|
| $S$ | 24 | 36 |
| $S'$ | 16 | 24 |

A student is chosen at random.

(a) Write down $\mathrm{P}(S)$. [1]

(b) Find $\mathrm{P}(G\mid S)$. [2]

(c) Show that the events $S$ and $G$ are independent. [3]
ms:
**(a)** $\dfrac{60}{100} = 0.6$ A1

**(b)** $\dfrac{24}{60}$ (M1)

$= 0.4$ A1

**(c)** $\mathrm{P}(G) = \dfrac{24 + 16}{100} = 0.4$ A1

$\mathrm{P}(S)\,\mathrm{P}(G) = 0.6\times 0.4 = 0.24$ M1

$\mathrm{P}(S\cap G) = \dfrac{24}{100} = 0.24 = \mathrm{P}(S)\,\mathrm{P}(G)$ R1

so $S$ and $G$ are independent AG

Alternative: $\mathrm{P}(G) = 0.4$ A1, $\mathrm{P}(G\mid S) = 0.4$ from (b) M1, $\mathrm{P}(G\mid S) = \mathrm{P}(G)$ R1 AG.

tname: Formal conditional probability and independence tests
text:
Events $A$ and $B$ have $\mathrm{P}(A) = x$, $\mathrm{P}(B) = 0.6$ and $\mathrm{P}(A\cup B) = 0.8$.

(a) Given that $A$ and $B$ are independent, find $x$. [3]

(b) Hence show that $A'$ and $B$ are also independent. [2]

(c) Find $x$ if, instead, $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive. [1]

(d) Explain why two events with non-zero probabilities cannot be both mutually exclusive and independent. [1]
ms:
**(a)** $x + 0.6 - 0.6x = 0.8$ M1A1

$0.4x = 0.2 \Rightarrow x = 0.5$ A1

**(b)** $\mathrm{P}(A'\cap B) = \mathrm{P}(B) - \mathrm{P}(A\cap B) = 0.6 - 0.3 = 0.3$ A1

$\mathrm{P}(A')\,\mathrm{P}(B) = 0.5\times 0.6 = 0.3$, these are equal R1

so $A'$ and $B$ are independent AG

**(c)** $x + 0.6 = 0.8 \Rightarrow x = 0.2$ A1

**(d)** mutually exclusive means $\mathrm{P}(A\cap B) = 0$, but independence requires $\mathrm{P}(A\cap B) = \mathrm{P}(A)\mathrm{P}(B) > 0$ R1

tname: Standardization of normal variables (z-values), inverse normal
text:
The random variable $X$ is normally distributed with mean 60 and standard deviation $\sigma$. It is known that $\mathrm{P}(X > 72) = 0.1$.

(a) Find the value of $\sigma$. [3]

(b) Find $\mathrm{P}(X < 50)$. [2]
ms:
**(a)** $\mathrm{P}\!\left(Z > \dfrac{72 - 60}{\sigma}\right) = 0.1$ (M1)

$\dfrac{12}{\sigma} = 1.28155\ldots$ A1

$\sigma = 9.36$ $(9.36364\ldots)$ A1

**(b)** $\mathrm{P}(X < 50)$ with $\sigma = 9.36364\ldots$ (M1)

$= 0.143$ $(0.142769\ldots)$ A1

FT from (a).

tname: Standardization of normal variables (z-values), inverse normal
text:
The random variable $X$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. It is known that $\mathrm{P}(X < 35) = 0.2$ and $\mathrm{P}(X > 60) = 0.05$.

(a) Find the value of $\mu$ and the value of $\sigma$. [5]

(b) Find $\mathrm{P}(40 < X < 50)$. [2]
ms:
**(a)** $\dfrac{35 - \mu}{\sigma} = -0.841621\ldots$ (M1)A1

$\dfrac{60 - \mu}{\sigma} = 1.64485\ldots$ A1

attempt to solve simultaneously (M1)

$\mu = 43.5$ $(43.4619\ldots)$, $\sigma = 10.1$ $(10.0543\ldots)$ A1

**(b)** $\mathrm{P}(40 < X < 50)$ (M1)

$= 0.377$ $(0.376938\ldots)$ A1

FT from (a).

tname: Standardization of normal variables (z-values), inverse normal
text:
Priya took a mathematics test and a history test. The scores on the mathematics test were normally distributed with mean 65 and standard deviation 8. The scores on the history test were normally distributed with mean 74 and standard deviation 5.

Priya scored 72 in mathematics and 80 in history.

(a) Find the $z$-score of Priya's mark in each test. [3]

(b) State, with a reason, in which test Priya performed better relative to the other students. [1]
ms:
**(a)** $z = \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$ (M1)

mathematics: $\dfrac{72 - 65}{8} = 0.875$ A1

history: $\dfrac{80 - 74}{5} = 1.2$ A1

**(b)** history, since her $z$-score there is higher (she is more standard deviations above the mean) R1

FT from (a).

tname: Standardization of normal variables (z-values), inverse normal
text:
A machine fills boxes with cereal. The mass, $X$ grams, of cereal in a box is normally distributed with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation 6 g. The label on each box states 500 g.

(a) Given that $\mu = 510$, find the probability that a box contains less than 500 g. [2]

The company wants only 2% of boxes to contain less than 500 g, as shown in the diagram.

![Normal curve with the region below 500 shaded, area 0.02](qbank/img/gen_math_SL4.12_4.svg)

(b) With $\sigma = 6$, find the value of $\mu$ needed. [3]

The company instead keeps $\mu = 510$ and buys a more precise machine, which reduces the standard deviation to $\sigma$ so that $\mathrm{P}(X < 500) = 0.02$.

(c) Find the value of $\sigma$. [3]

For parts (d) and (e), use $\mu = 510$ and your value of $\sigma$ from (c).

(d) A shop buys 15 boxes. Find the probability that at most one box contains less than 500 g. [3]

(e) A box is found to contain more than 505 g. Find the probability that it contains more than 515 g. [3]
